query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing treatment to an as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy refines its inherent lamellar microstructure into a hierarchical ultrafine duplex architecture that increases both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (for example, AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a coarse lamellar or dual-phase (soft FCC and hard BCC/B2) structure with limited interfacial density.
generation.intervention: A single thermo-mechanical processing step consisting of cryogenic rolling (to introduce severe plastic deformation) followed by a controlled annealing treatment to induce nano-scale grain refinement and phase decomposition.
generation.conditions: Processing performed in an inert atmosphere with cryogenic rolling at sub-ambient temperatures and subsequent annealing at a temperature low enough to prevent coarsening, with final mechanical tests conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The refined hierarchical lamellar interfaces and ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure (e.g., nanoscale FCC matrix interspersed with fine, coherent hard phase precipitates) that serve both as barriers to dislocation motion and facilitators of strain accommodation.
generation.mechanism: The intervention increases the density of coherent phase boundaries that block dislocation motion (raising strength) while simultaneously creating strain gradients that promote uniform plastic flow and microcrack arresting (preserving or enhancing ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated, as-cast alloy, the treated material should exhibit a measurable improvement in yield strength (for instance, on the order of 20% or greater) while maintaining or even slightly increasing elongation to failure, thereby breaking the conventional trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-cast eutectic HEA, which typically shows a trade-off behavior with either high strength at the expense of ductility or vice versa due to its coarse lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the rolling reduction and annealing parameters are optimized to avoid over-annealing (which would coarsen the microstructure) or excessive deformation (which might induce damage), so the intervention may not be effective if processing parameters fall outside the optimal window.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on the specific processing conditions, alloy composition, and scale of microstructural refinement. Further experiments are needed to refine the processing window and fully decouple the contributions from interface strengthening versus ductile deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set remains in the as-cast state as a control, while the experimental set undergoes the defined cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing. Characterize their microstructures using TEM/SEM and XRD to confirm the formation of a refined hierarchical duplex structure, and then perform tensile tests at room temperature to measure yield strength and elongation.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing via TEM/SEM
Phase distribution and coherency via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and ductility (elongation) relative to the as-cast control— or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the predicted hierarchical, refined duplex architecture—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
